title: Baal and Asherah
lead: Baal, the Canaanite storm god who was thought to bring rain and life, and the goddesses Asherah and Astarte were Israel's chief rivals for worship from the judges to the exile. The Bible tells the long contest, from Gideon's torn-down altar to Elijah on Mount Carmel.

sections.b:
The word ba'al means "owner, lord, husband." In the Ugarit texts from Syria (about 1300 BC) Baal is the storm god Hadad, who defeats Sea and Death and brings the rain. In the Bible "the Baals" are his local forms, such as Baal-peor (Numbers 25:3) and Baal-berith, "Baal of the covenant," at Shechem (Judges 8:33; Judges 9:4). Asherah was a mother goddess, and an asherah was also a wooden pole or tree set up for her near altars (Deuteronomy 16:21; Judges 6:25–26). Ashtoreth is the Hebrew form of Astarte, a goddess of war and love.

Judges names the Baals and the Ashtoreths as the reason for Israel's repeated troubles (Judges 2:11–13; Judges 10:6). Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and earns the name Jerubbaal, "let Baal contend" (Judges 6:25–32). Elijah's contest on Carmel asks who really sends rain (1 Kings 18). Hosea says Israel did not know that the LORD, not Baal, gave her grain, wine and oil (Hosea 2:8), and looks for a day when she will no longer call God "my Baal" (Hosea 2:16). Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud (about 800 BC) that speak of "Yahweh and his asherah" show how the two worships could mix.
